title: LIKE
description: Match SQL text with LIKE, percent and underscore wildcards, explicit escaping, and bound patterns; understand collation and prefix-search limits.
notes:
## Patterns describe a shape rather than one value

LIKE tests text against a pattern containing ordinary characters and simple wildcards. A campus equipment catalogue might group products whose names begin with Pro. Equality with Pro would match only the complete value under the relevant comparison rules, while a prefix pattern can also match ProCamera and ProMicrophone. The correct operator follows the requested search shape.

A pattern is not a regular expression. LIKE has its own small wildcard language, and a symbol meaningful in a regular expression can be ordinary text here. Keeping the languages distinct prevents a student from writing a dot-star expression and expecting it to behave like a SQL percent wildcard. Choose the simplest supported language that expresses the actual requirement.

## Percent admits an empty sequence too

The percent wildcard matches a sequence of zero or more characters. A pattern beginning with Pro and ending with percent therefore matches Pro itself as well as longer values with that prefix. Do not assume that at least one extra character is required. Include the bare prefix in fixtures so that misunderstanding becomes visible rather than hidden by examples containing only longer names.

Percent at the beginning changes the question to a suffix or substring search. A pattern with percent before book matches values ending in book. With percent on both sides, it can match book anywhere in the value. Those searches are useful but broader than a prefix search. A misplaced wildcard can return plausible catalogue rows while violating a precise naming rule.

## Underscore consumes one character

The underscore wildcard matches exactly one character. A pattern consisting of one underscore followed by ovel matches a five-character value whose last four characters are ovel. It does not match ovel itself, because the first position still needs a character. It also does not match a longer prefix unless the rest of the pattern allows those additional positions.

Combine underscore and percent deliberately. Pro followed by underscore requires at least one character after Pro and permits exactly one if nothing follows that underscore. Pro followed by underscore and percent requires at least one extra character but can admit more. These distinctions are easiest to understand by tracing each pattern token against the text rather than memorizing a few familiar examples.

```sql
SELECT equipment_id, name
FROM equipment_names
WHERE name LIKE 'Pro%'
ORDER BY equipment_id;
```

## The whole string must fit the pattern

LIKE does not ordinarily mean find this fragment anywhere unless the pattern includes wildcards that allow the surrounding text. A pattern Camera contains no wildcard and must fit the complete value according to its comparison semantics. It does not automatically match NewCamera. To search for that fragment within a larger value, supply the intended surrounding percent wildcards.

This makes prefix, suffix and containment separate feature choices. A search box labeled starts with should not silently construct a containment pattern because that returns more results. A literal-name comparison may be better expressed with equality when no wildcard semantics are intended. State whether a caller is submitting raw search text or an actual pattern language.

## Literal wildcard characters need escaping

Sometimes the text being sought contains a percent or underscore as data. A label beginning with 50% must distinguish a literal percent sign from a wildcard. MySQL supports an ESCAPE clause that names the escape character. Using an explicit exclamation mark makes the example easier to read without depending on layers of backslash interpretation in SQL string literals.

```sql
SELECT label_id, label
FROM catalogue_labels
WHERE label LIKE '50!%%' ESCAPE '!'
ORDER BY label_id;
```

In this pattern, the first percent is escaped and therefore literal; the final percent remains a wildcard. The escape character itself also needs the appropriate treatment when searched literally. A user-input helper should handle the escape character as well as percent and underscore according to a documented algorithm. Otherwise an input containing the chosen escape marker can change the intended pattern.

## Parameter binding does not escape the pattern language

Binding a search value prevents it from becoming SQL structure through unsafe string concatenation. It does not make percent and underscore literal inside a LIKE pattern. If the UI promises a literal prefix search, escape pattern metacharacters in the user's text before adding the deliberate trailing wildcard, then bind the resulting pattern through the supported client API.

If the UI intentionally supports wildcard patterns, validate length and communicate the feature clearly. The caller's ability to supply a wildcard is a product decision rather than a side effect of forgetting to escape input. Keep access enforcement at the trusted data boundary regardless of the search form. A broader pattern must not expose rows the caller lacks permission to read.

## Text comparison rules still apply

LIKE case behaviour depends on the applicable character types and [collation](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/data-types) rather than a universal case-insensitive promise. A pattern Pro can distinguish pro under one declared comparison contract and match it under another. The literal-percent exercise uses an explicit ASCII binary collation for its limited synthetic labels. The retained catalogue exercise preserves its original schema and avoids case-ambiguous fixture values.

Character encoding and collation also affect more than case. An underscore represents a character rather than a blanket promise about one raw byte of a multibyte encoding. Trailing spaces can behave differently from assumptions drawn from ordinary equality. Test the actual text contract, especially when importing labels from several systems or offering searches across languages with different comparison needs.

## Missing text is not an empty string

A [NULL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/null-values) value compared through LIKE yields an unknown result and does not survive an ordinary positive WHERE condition. An empty string is known text containing zero characters. A pattern consisting only of percent can match that empty string because the wildcard permits an empty sequence. It still does not turn a NULL source value into an accepted empty value.

NOT LIKE also leaves an unknown result unknown. If a report should include both known nonmatching names and missing names, add the missing-name condition explicitly. A catalogue cleanup report may need that broad population, while a product search normally should not. The same operator supports different useful features when their missing-value policies are stated clearly.

## Search shape influences access strategies

A fixed left prefix can sometimes support an index range strategy on an appropriate index. A leading wildcard generally prevents that straightforward prefix-range lookup, although other access paths can still be considered. Do not promise that every prefix search uses an index or that every containment search must use one specific physical plan. Types, collation, selectivity and available indexes matter.

Measure representative queries when search cost becomes important. A short substring on a large catalogue can match many rows and require substantial scanning or filtering. Bound result retrieval according to the feature's contract, and retain deterministic ordering for the displayed page. LIMIT controls output size; it does not prove that the database examined only that many candidate rows.

## Keep normalization visible to callers

Trimming leading spaces or converting names to lowercase can change what a prefix search means. If a stored label begins with a space, an exact prefix query should not quietly treat that space as absent unless normalization is part of the search contract. Apply a consistent rule to indexed search values and displayed explanations. Otherwise users can see a returned label that appears not to satisfy the prefix they entered.

## Do not silently promote LIKE into validation

A simple pattern can identify a prefix or approximate naming shape, but it may not fully validate a structured identifier. Requiring exactly three uppercase letters and four digits is more naturally expressed through an appropriate regular expression and trusted validation rules. Conversely, a prefix catalogue filter does not need a complex regular expression merely because the engine offers one.

The first exercise preserves the existing product-prefix task and includes the bare prefix and a prefix appearing later in the string. Its original text comparison settings remain intact. The second searches for a literal percent sign before an arbitrary suffix. Together they expose wildcard placement, empty-sequence behaviour and escaping mistakes. Explain the pattern as a sequence of literal and wildcard tokens, then test its result against both obvious matches and near misses.

questions.question_text: What does % match in LIKE?
questions.explanation: The empty suffix is permitted.

questions.question_text: What does _ match in LIKE?
questions.explanation: It consumes one character position.

questions.question_text: Which pattern expresses a Pro prefix?
questions.explanation: The trailing percent allows the suffix.

questions.question_text: Why can a leading wildcard cost more than a fixed prefix search?
options: It generally prevents a straightforward left-prefix index range lookup
questions.explanation: Actual plans still depend on the complete query and indexes.

questions.question_text: How can a pattern search for a literal percent?
options: Assume two percent signs are literal
Escape it using the declared pattern escape convention
questions.explanation: An explicit ESCAPE clause makes the convention visible.

questions.question_text: What influences LIKE case sensitivity?
options: The applicable text comparison and collation rules
questions.explanation: Declare and test the intended text semantics.

questions.question_text: What shape does _ovel describe?
options: Exactly five characters with any first character then ovel
questions.explanation: No wildcard permits extra leading or trailing characters.

questions.question_text: Can a fixed-prefix pattern sometimes use an appropriate index efficiently?
options: No, LIKE can never use indexes
Yes, but inspect the actual plan rather than guarantee it
Only if there is no collation
questions.explanation: A prefix shape can support a range strategy.

questions.question_text: Does Pro% match the complete value Pro?
options: No, one extra character is required
questions.explanation: Percent accepts an empty sequence.

questions.question_text: What does Pro_ require when no other tokens follow?
options: Any number after Pro including zero
questions.explanation: The underscore consumes exactly one position.

questions.question_text: What does Pro_% require?
options: At least one character after Pro
Only a literal percent at the end
questions.explanation: The underscore requires one and percent allows the remainder.

questions.question_text: Does LIKE Camera automatically match NewCamera?
options: No, surrounding text needs an allowing wildcard
questions.explanation: The pattern must fit the complete text.

questions.question_text: In 50!%% ESCAPE ! with the SQL literals supplied correctly, what is literal?
options: The first percent after the escape marker
questions.explanation: The final unescaped percent remains the suffix wildcard.

questions.question_text: Does parameter binding make user-supplied % literal inside LIKE?
options: No, SQL binding and pattern escaping solve different problems
Yes, every bound string loses wildcard semantics
Only when the placeholder is named
questions.explanation: Escape pattern syntax when the feature promises literal text.

questions.question_text: What else must a literal-search escaping helper handle?
questions.explanation: Otherwise an input escape marker can alter pattern interpretation.

questions.question_text: Does a NULL name match a pattern of only % in WHERE?
options: Only if there are no other rows
questions.explanation: Missing text is not an empty string.

questions.question_text: Can an empty non-NULL string match %?
options: No, every match needs one character
questions.explanation: Percent can match zero characters.

questions.question_text: Does NOT LIKE automatically include missing names?
questions.explanation: Add IS NULL if that population is required.

questions.question_text: What does LIMIT on a containment search fail to prove?
options: That the result has a bound
That only that many candidates were examined
questions.explanation: Output size and search effort are distinct.

questions.question_text: Which search is a good use of simple LIKE?
options: An exact uppercase-letter and digit grammar with alternatives
A literal prefix with an arbitrary suffix
questions.explanation: Choose a language proportional to the actual shape.

coding_problems.title: Names Starting with Pro
coding_problems.task: Return id,name for products whose name begins with Pro using LIKE 'Pro%', ordered by id. Keep the retained schema, sample and comparison settings. Case behaviour follows the configured text collation; fixtures avoid mixed-case ambiguity. The bare name Pro qualifies.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE products (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  category TEXT NOT NULL,
  price INTEGER NOT NULL,
  stock INTEGER
);
coding_problems.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
(1, 'ProLaptop', 'Electronics', 85000, 12),
(2, 'Notebook', 'Stationery', 40, NULL),
(3, 'Python Basics', 'Books', 350, 5),
(4, 'ProPhone', 'Electronics', 45000, 0),
(5, 'Novel', 'Books', 220, NULL),
(6, 'Desk Lamp', 'Home', 900, 8);
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A name containing Pro only later is excluded.
hints: Place percent after the fixed prefix.
Keep the original output id ordering.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT id,name FROM products WHERE name LIKE 'Pro%' ORDER BY id;
coding_problems.explanation: The fixed prefix and trailing wildcard match the retained catalogue names. Percent accepts an empty suffix; a later occurrence of Pro is not enough. This retained schema does not declare a universal case-sensitive collation.

validation_cases.seed_sql:
INSERT INTO products (id, name, category, price, stock) VALUES
(1, 'ProTablet', 'Electronics', 32000, 4),
(2, 'Pencil Set', 'Stationery', 60, NULL),
(3, 'SQL Guide', 'Books', 500, 10),
(4, 'ProSpeaker', 'Electronics', 6000, 0);

coding_problems.title: Search labels beginning with literal 50 percent
coding_problems.task: Return label_id,label where label begins with the exact literal characters 50% and may have any suffix. Use ESCAPE '!' so the percent in the prefix is literal and a later percent remains the suffix wildcard. Order by label_id.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE catalogue_labels(label_id INT PRIMARY KEY,label VARCHAR(50) CHARACTER SET ascii COLLATE ascii_bin);
coding_problems.ordering: As explicitly ordered in the result query.
constraints: Use only the supplied synthetic tables and requested transition.
edge_cases: A label consisting of exactly 50% qualifies.
A numeric-looking 500 prefix must not qualify.
hints: Separate the literal percent from the suffix wildcard.
Use the explicit single-character escape convention.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT label_id,label FROM catalogue_labels WHERE label LIKE '50!%%' ESCAPE '!' ORDER BY label_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The escape marker makes the first percent literal. The final unescaped percent admits zero or more suffix characters without broadening the required prefix.

original_questions.question_text: What does the % wildcard match in a LIKE pattern?
options: Any sequence of zero or more characters
original_questions.explanation: % matches any run of characters, including none at all.

original_questions.question_text: What does the _ wildcard match in a LIKE pattern?
original_questions.explanation: _ matches precisely one character, no more and no fewer.

original_questions.question_text: Which pattern matches strings that START with 'Pro'?
original_questions.explanation: A trailing % after the fixed prefix matches anything starting with 'Pro'.

original_questions.question_text: Why can a leading % in a LIKE pattern (e.g. '%book%') hurt performance on large tables?
options: The database can't know where in the string to start looking, generally preventing efficient use of a normal index
It always causes a syntax error on large tables specifically
original_questions.explanation: Without a fixed starting point, an index that's sorted by the column's value can't narrow the search efficiently.

original_questions.question_text: How can you match a literal '%' character rather than using it as a wildcard?
options: Using an ESCAPE clause, e.g. LIKE '50\%%' ESCAPE '\'
By using two percent signs together
By switching to the = operator instead
original_questions.explanation: Most dialects support an ESCAPE clause to treat a wildcard character as a literal.

original_questions.question_text: Does LIKE's case sensitivity come from LIKE itself or from something else?
options: LIKE is always case-sensitive by definition
It depends on the column's collation setting, the same as ordinary comparison operators
LIKE is always case-insensitive by definition
Case sensitivity is randomly determined per query
original_questions.explanation: Collation governs case-sensitivity for LIKE just as it does for =, not a property of LIKE itself.

options: A string of exactly 5 characters, with any first character followed by 'ovel'
original_questions.explanation: _ requires exactly one character in that position, followed by the literal 'ovel'.

original_questions.question_text: Does a trailing-only wildcard pattern like 'book%' have the same indexing limitation as a leading wildcard?
options: No — a trailing-only wildcard can typically still use a normal index efficiently, unlike a leading wildcard
Trailing wildcards are not supported by LIKE
Both patterns always require a full table scan
original_questions.explanation: Because the fixed prefix gives the index a starting point, trailing-wildcard patterns are generally index-friendly.
